mcqs.question: What problem does Unicode solve that ASCII and code pages couldn't?
options: Unicode assigns a single, unambiguous code point to every character across every script, instead of different code pages reusing the same byte values for different characters
Unicode makes text files smaller than ASCII
Unicode removes the need for any encoding when storing text as bytes
Unicode only works for European languages, same as ASCII
mcqs.explanation: The core problem with code pages was ambiguity -- the same byte value meant a different character depending on which code page was assumed. Unicode fixes this by giving every character one unambiguous code point; how those code points become bytes is still a separate encoding question (UTF-8, etc).

mcqs.question: In UTF-8, how can you tell that a byte is a continuation byte rather than the start of a character?
options: Continuation bytes are always 0x00
A continuation byte's top two bits are always 10, distinguishing it from every leading-byte pattern
Continuation bytes only appear at the end of a string
There's no way to tell without decoding from the start of the string
mcqs.explanation: UTF-8 reserves the bit pattern 10xxxxxx exclusively for continuation bytes -- no leading byte ever starts with those two bits, which is exactly what lets you find a character boundary starting from any byte position.

mcqs.question: Why is truncating a UTF-8 string at a fixed byte offset risky?
options: UTF-8 strings cannot be truncated at all
Byte-offset truncation only works for UTF-16, not UTF-8
The cut point can fall in the middle of a multi-byte character, producing invalid or corrupted text
It always deletes the first character of the string instead of the last
mcqs.explanation: Since UTF-8 characters can span 1 to 4 bytes, cutting at an arbitrary byte offset can slice through a multi-byte sequence, leaving a broken partial character (and sometimes invalid UTF-8) at the boundary.

mcqs.question: Why does a JavaScript string holding one emoji report `.length === 2` instead of 1?
options: JavaScript strings are UTF-16 internally, and that emoji's code point needs a surrogate pair -- two 16-bit code units -- so length counts 2 code units, not 1 character
JavaScript always doubles the length of any string containing non-ASCII characters
The emoji is stored twice in memory for rendering redundancy
This only happens on Windows; other platforms report length 1
mcqs.explanation: `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. Code points outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (most emoji) require a surrogate pair of two code units, so length reports 2 even though a user sees one character. Iterating by code point (`[...s]`) gets the count right; indexing by code unit can split the pair and produce an invalid half-character.

mcqs.question: Why does UTF-16 need a byte order mark (BOM) while UTF-8 doesn't strictly require one?
options: UTF-16 encodes each code unit as multiple bytes whose order (big- or little-endian) must be signaled, while UTF-8's byte sequence has only one valid order to begin with
UTF-8 files are never allowed to contain a BOM under the Unicode standard
UTF-16 files are always exactly 2 bytes long, so no order needs specifying
The BOM is required by all encodings to mark the start of a file
mcqs.explanation: UTF-16's multi-byte code units raise the same endianness question as any multi-byte value, so the BOM lets a reader detect byte order by checking for U+FEFF versus the swapped U+FFFE. UTF-8's byte sequence is unambiguous regardless of platform endianness, so it needs no such marker -- though some tools prepend one anyway out of convention, which can itself cause parsing bugs.
